about: SEA CARDS: THE SEA (Design/content/BRIEF.md and BRIEF_2.md; Design/npc_text_encounters.md 2.1-2.8, 4.2 and sample 6). 63 cards of stage 'sea': what happens between ports, drawn from the weather, the hour, the month, the year, the kind of water (level_kind: ocean or river_place), the days at sea and what is in the hold. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. Every *_key has real words in Data/writing/sea.json; 'title', 'intention' and 'label' repeat those words so the panel shows them before the writing is merged. HOW THEY COME: 'rate' is per game hour under way (a third of it at anchor); a card with no rate comes only as another card's 'then'. The rates of all cards add up to 5.06 an hour, but most are shut by their 'when' at any one time; in fair weather on the open sea in summer about 0.07 to 0.10 an hour is open (two or three cards on a first crossing of thirty hours, fewer once the cool-downs run). To make the sea quieter or busier, scale every rate. ODDS: each option's label ends in its odds as a word, (sure), (likely) or (doubtful), worked out from its chance at a middling crew (sure from 0.8, likely from 0.55: knowing_793.json); the panel also adds the engine's own word to an option with a chance (EncounterPanel.cs), so one of the two should go when the writing is merged. OUTCOMES: the engine says what an option did as plain facts from its effects; sea.json also has written outcomes under <label_key>.done, or <label_key>.success and <label_key>.failure for a chance, which the panel does not show yet (see 'needs' in the writer's report). EVERY DANGER WARNS FIRST AND WOUNDS BEFORE IT KILLS: the gale needs the swell's flag (sea_gale_warned), the thick fog the bank's (sea_fog_warned), the gaining leak the weeping seam's or a grounding's (sea_leak), the split sail the open seam's (sea_sail_weak), thirst the bad cask's (sea_short_water), blows the quarrel's (sea_quarrel); a man can be lost (men -1) on two cards only, sea.overboard.chilled and sea.sick.worse, each of which waits for the flag of an earlier wound and offers a sure way out. No card takes the boat: the sea itself does that, in the ship's physics. Every card has an option that is always open and costs nothing but time or pride. FLAGS (all begin sea_): warnings and wounds as above; sea_reefed, sea_lashed (made ready: better roads in the gale, no shifting cargo); sea_marks_taken (a good mark within the day: the sure road in fog, no wrong headland); sea_bar_known (a fisherman's word of the channel); sea_spar_aboard (a jury sail); sea_knows_sun, sea_knows_star, sea_knows_birds, sea_knows_lead (lessons, kept for good); sea_after_gale (survivors likelier); and for harbour cards to read: sea_vow_penny, sea_vow_altar, sea_broke_fast, sea_cask_short, sea_carried_dead, sea_saved_lives, sea_saw_raid, sea_season_closing. THE CREW: the steersman (a Frisian, Christian), the lookout (the youngest hand) and the hand (an old Dane who keeps the old gods and speaks Frisian aboard) are fixed actors with no port, so the same three people speak on every card and remember what the merchant chose; when the crew become real people these three roles should be filled from them. SOURCES are in each card's 'note'; (?) marks what is not verified.

cards.note: THE WARNING before sea.gale.breaks (which needs flag sea_gale_warned). The sign is the weather document's: a long swell from a quarter the wind is not blowing from, the cloud lowering, gulls going inland (Design/weather_and_sea_state.md 3; playability_and_fun.md 2.4). It comes while the weather's storm is building (storm between 0.1 and 0.5) and the gale has not yet broken. No direction is named because the cards cannot read the wind's quarter. Jarrow: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 794, the heathen ships broken by storm at Donemuthe (chronicle_793.json 794-summer-donemuthe-raid). Reefing: reef points on these sails are reconstructed, not found (ship_physics.md 1.5).

cards.note: The gale, after its warning (sea.swell.long sets sea_gale_warned). It wounds and does not kill: the sea itself, in the ship's physics, is what can take the boat (playability_and_fun.md 2.4: a Gislinge boat lives through force 7-8 reefed and running for a lee). Lying head to sea under oars, and running under a scrap of sail: ship_physics.md 1.5 and 2.10. The goods lost are whatever is lowest and spoils wet: salt and grain, if aboard.

cards.note: THE LEAD AND THE LOOK OF THE WATER. Sounding is in Acts 27:28-29 (twenty fathoms, then fifteen; four anchors cast from the stern), which a Christian steersman would have heard read. Old English glosses of c. 1000 have sundgyrd (sounding rod) and sundline (sounding line) (?); the lead's use in northern waters in 793 is unproven and is kept as the game's tool (playability_and_fun.md 1.4). cards.note: BEACON SMOKE ASHORE, read three ways. In 800 Charles went along the coast, set up a fleet and posted guards against the pirates (Annales regni Francorum 800, in our words; chronicle_793.json 800-03-channel-coastguard), and in 802 the coast-dwellers were to be ready to muster: that the watchers signalled by smoke is our guess (?); the coast guard is not heard of after the 830s, so the line changes after 840. Salt was boiled from peat along the Frisian and Zeeland shore (wildlife_and_seasons.md 2.10 salt_fires; a Lorsch charter of 776 for salt pans in Zeeland (?)). The bad road shows a raid and costs nothing but nerve: the raiders themselves belong to the raider sim.

cards.note: A SAIL MADE OUT, and what the lookout says of her. Raiders go out about the first of May and are home before October (Plans/ai_fleets.md), so the lookout's doubt is a summer doubt. Portland: three ships of Northmen came in Beorhtric's days, 'and then the reeve rode to the place, and would have driven them to the king's town, because he knew not who they were: and they there slew him' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787 for 789, tr. Giles 1847, wording to check (?); Aethelweard names him Beaduheard and says he took them for merchants). 810: a Danish fleet of 200 ships in Frisia, and Godfred killed (Annales regni Francorum 810). 834: Dorestad sacked (Annales Bertiniani). The stranger on the bad road is never named: the wound is a hard row.

cards.note: THE MIDNIGHT LIGHT IN THE NORTH. steersman.name: Aldger
steersman.note: The Frisian at the side rudder: dry, careful, a Christian who has heard the readings.

lookout.name: Beornwine
lookout.note: The youngest hand, in the bow: sharp eyes, quick mouth.

cards.title: The sail splits
cards.intention: With a crack like a dropped plank the sail splits from the foot to the yard. Two halves stream out downwind, thrashing, and the boat falls off into the trough.

options.label: Get it down, hold her head to the sea, and sew (sure)
Set the sound half on the spar you picked up (sure)
Run on under what is left of it (doubtful)

cards.note: Cargo shifting in a seaway (trim and the loose weight to leeward: ship_physics.md 2.3). It never comes when the cargo was lashed on a warning (flag sea_lashed, from sea.swell.long, sea.sky.ring or sea.porpoise.roll). Mayen quernstones are Dorestad's great heavy cargo (goods_793.json quernstones, a pair, 12 d).
cards.when: under_way and wind >= 9 and hold.value > 0 and not flag.sea_lashed

lookout.name: Beornwine

cards.title: The cargo moves
cards.intention: On a hard roll something heavy slides in the hold and fetches up against the lee side with a thump that everyone feels in their feet. She does not come all the way back upright.

options.label: Bring her head to the wind and restow (sure)
Put the stones that moved over the side (sure)
Trim her with the men's weight and sail on (likely)

cards.note: Wine in the hold. 'Wine is the lord's and the Mass's drink; ale and mead are everyone's' (BRIEF rule 2). A cask of Rhenish is about 60 d (goods_793.json rhenish_wine). The Dane's verse is Havamal 11: 'Worse food for the journey he brings not afield than an over-drinking of ale' (tr. Bellows 1923: texts_793.json havamal_011, given by the third option). The short cask sets flag sea_cask_short for a buyer's card to notice.
cards.when: under_way and hold.rhenish_wine > 0 and days_at_sea >= 1

steersman.note: The Frisian at the side rudder: dry, careful, a Christian who has heard the readings.

hand.name: Ravn
hand.note: The old hand, a Dane who has sailed in Frisian boats for years and speaks their tongue aboard; he keeps the old gods and says less than he means.

cards.title: A cask is weeping
cards.intention: One of the wine casks is weeping at a stave. There is a red stain down its side, a smell over the whole boat, and three men have found reasons to be standing next to it.

options.label: Drive the hoops down and stop it with tallow (sure)
Draw a jug for the men before you stop it (sure)
It is leaking anyway: let them finish the cask (sure)

cards.note: A MAN OVERBOARD. He is always got back on this card: the warning and the wound. Only the next card (sea.overboard.chilled, flag sea_man_chilled) can lose him. Breca is the youth Beowulf swam against for five nights (Beowulf fitts IX-X: texts_793.json beowulf_09). North Sea water is 6 C in winter and 17 C in summer (weather_and_sea_state.md 1.3).
cards.when: under_way and wind >= 7 and crew >= 3

hand.name: Ravn
hand.note: The old hand, a Dane who has sailed in Frisian boats for years and speaks their tongue aboard; he keeps the old gods and says less than he means.

cards.title: A man in the sea
cards.intention: A sea lifts the bow, the youngest hand is standing where he should be sitting, and then he is not in the boat. His head comes up a spear's cast astern with his mouth open.

options.label: Down sail, out oars, and pull back for him (sure)
Throw him the bailer on its line (doubtful)
Throw him an oar to hold, and bring her round under sail (likely)

cards.note: After the rescue: the cold. Here, and only after the first card's wound, a man can be lost, and only by the risky choice; the plain choice is sure and costs half a day. The steersman's saying is what seamen have always told of men taken from cold water; nothing of our period records it (?).
cards.when: flag.sea_man_chilled

steersman.name: Aldger
steersman.note: The Frisian at the side rudder: dry, careful, a Christian who has heard the readings.

cards.title: He has stopped shivering
cards.intention: The man you pulled out of the sea is lying in the bottom of the boat with his knees drawn up to his chin. He has stopped shivering, which the steersman says is worse than shivering. His lips are the colour of slate.

options.label: Strip him, wrap him in every dry cloak, and put a man on each side (sure)
Broach a cask of ale and get some into him (likely)
Put him back on an oar to warm himself (doubtful)

cards.note: SICKNESS: THE WARNING before sea.sick.worse (flag sea_fever). The steersman's line is the design's own (npc_text_encounters.md sample 21: 'the old man says bleed him; the priest says pray'). The marsh fever of the delta, the Fens and the Thames marsh comes in the warm months (wildlife_and_seasons.md 2.10 ague); Old English lencten-adl, the spring fever, in the 9th-century leechbooks (?).
cards.when: under_way and days_at_sea >= 3 and crew >= 3 and not flag.sea_fever

hand.name: Ravn

cards.title: A man with fever
cards.intention: One of the men did not get up for his turn at the oar. He is hot to the touch, his teeth are knocking together, and he says the boat is full of people he knows.

lines.when: level_kind = river_place and month >= 5 and month <= 9

options.label: Rest him in the stern under a cloak, with water (likely)
Keep him at his oar: he can sweat it out (doubtful)
Put in to the nearest landing and find him a roof (sure)

cards.note: The fever, after its warning. Here, and only by the risky choice, a man can die (men -1); the plain choice costs a week and is sure. Bloodletting: Bede tells of a nun bled on the wrong day of the moon (Historia ecclesiastica V.3), and the leechbooks give the days. A vow to a saint in sickness at sea is the commonest miracle story of the age; the vow sets flag sea_vow_altar for a harbour card to collect.
cards.when: flag.sea_fever

cards.title: The sick man is worse
cards.intention: The sick man is worse. He no longer knows the boat. He has not kept water down since yesterday, and the others have moved their sleeping places away from him without anyone saying to.

options.label: Make for the nearest roof, whatever shore it is (sure)
Bleed him, as the old men say (doubtful)
Vow an offering at the next altar, and nurse him as you can (likely)

cards.note: SHORT WATER: THE WARNING before sea.water.thirst (flag sea_short_water). The boat carries four casks of sixty litres, three litres a man a day, water first and then the ale (voyage_rules.json). NEEDS a water variable and a water effect: the encounter engine cannot read or change the casks tonight, so the card makes its own fact (one cask spoiled) and its cost is health and heart.
cards.when: under_way and days_at_sea >= 2 and not flag.sea_short_water

cards.title: Bad water
cards.intention: One of the water casks has gone bad. What comes out of it is green, smells like a harbour at low tide, and has things in it that swim. The others are not full.

options.label: Put in for water at the first stream (sure)
Ration it: a cup a man, morning and evening (sure)
Broach a cask of the ale instead (sure)

cards.note: Thirst, after its warning: it wounds (health, heart) and does not kill on the card; the voyage rules take a quarter of the crew's health for each day with nothing to drink (voyage_rules.json thirst_per_day). Digging for sweet water behind the dunes is how the coast is watered still.
cards.when: under_way and flag.sea_short_water

steersman.name: Aldger
steersman.note: The Frisian at the side rudder: dry, careful, a Christian who has heard the readings.

cards.title: The last of the water
cards.intention: The cask is down to the dregs. Tongues are thick, lips are split, and nobody has spat over the side all day.

options.label: Land wherever there is green, and dig above the tide line (sure)
Spread the sail for dew and rain, and hold on (doubtful)
Hail the first boat you see and buy water, for two pennies (likely)

cards.note: A QUARREL OVER THE STEERING OAR: THE WARNING before sea.quarrel.blows (flag sea_quarrel). The side rudder hangs on the starboard quarter, the 'steering board' side (Old English steorbord), worked by a tiller (ship_physics.md 1.5, 2.7). The two crewmen remember what the merchant chose.
cards.when: under_way and days_at_sea >= 2 and crew >= 3 and not flag.sea_quarrel

cards.title: Two hands on the oar
cards.intention: The lookout says the steersman has let her fall off to leeward all morning. The steersman says a boy who has steered nothing bigger than a ferry should keep his eyes on the sea and his mouth for eating. Both have a hand on the steering oar.

options.label: Back the steersman: the oar is his (sure)
Give the boy a spell at the oar under the steersman's eye (likely)
Say nothing and let them settle it (sure)

memory.back: backed the steersman over the oar
memory.turn.success: gave the boy the oar, and he steered well
memory.turn.failure: gave the boy the oar, and he put her aback
memory.leave: let the quarrel over the oar lie

cards.note: The quarrel, after its warning: the wound is to the men's feelings and the boat's heart. The Dane's island is the holmgang, the duel on an islet or a pegged cloak, known from the later sagas and law (Kormaks saga 10 (?)); for the 790s it is a guess.

cards.title: It comes to hands
cards.intention: It has come to hands. The boy has a split lip, the steersman has him by the hair over the gunwale, and the boat is steering herself.

options.label: Take the oar yourself and order them apart (sure)
Dock them both a day's share for the ship's peace (sure)
Broach a cask of ale and make them clasp hands over it (likely)

memory.part: was ordered apart in the fight over the oar
memory.fine: was docked a day's share for fighting

cards.note: The night watch. Four men and a merchant sail day and night on a crossing of thirty hours (playability_and_fun.md 1.2-1.3): somebody steers while the rest sleep.
cards.when: under_way and hour >= 1 and hour < 4 and days_at_sea >= 1

steersman.name: Aldger
steersman.note: The Frisian at the side rudder: dry, careful, a Christian who has heard the readings.

cards.title: Asleep at the oar
cards.intention: You wake in the dead of the night to a different motion. The boat is lying across the sea with the sail slatting, and the man at the steering oar is asleep on his feet with his arm hooked over the tiller.

options.label: Take the oar yourself till dawn, and let him sleep (sure)
Wake him with a bailer of sea water (sure)
Rouse the whole boat and shame him (sure)

cards.note: FINDING THE WAY BY THE SUN. 'The heading was kept by the sun and the land, the position found by landfall'; no compass and no chart before 1066; the sun-board and the sunstone are later or disputed and are not used (playability_and_fun.md 1.4, 3.2: 'a noon sun is south'). The dark sun: after the blinding of Constantine VI in August 797 'the sun was darkened for seventeen days and did not give its rays, so that ships lost their course' (Theophanes, Chronographia, AM 6289, our rendering; chronicle_793.json 797-08-sun-darkened). The lesson sets flag sea_knows_sun, which makes the first option sure for ever after.
cards.when: under_way and level_kind = ocean and days_at_sea >= 1 and fog < 0.6 and storm < 0.3 and hour >= 10 and hour < 14 and not flag.sea_marks_taken

steersman.name: Aldger
steersman.note: The Frisian at the side rudder: dry, careful, a Christian who has heard the readings.

cards.title: Nothing but sea
cards.intention: No land on any side since yesterday. The sea is the same in every direction, the wind has shifted twice in the night, and it is near noon with the sun out.

options.label: Take the noon shadow yourself, as he taught you (sure)
Have the steersman find south, and show you how (likely)
Keep the wind on the same cheek and trust it (doubtful)

memory.ask.success: asked to be shown the noon sun
memory.ask.failure: asked to be shown the noon sun

cards.note: Steering by the pole star. Old English scip-steorra, 'ship-star', is glossed as the pole star and the Wain is Carles waen, in texts of c. 1000 (?); the Norse 'Wagon' likewise. In 800 the star now called Polaris stood nearly seven degrees from the true pole (precession), so it 'hardly moved' rather than stood still: the game's sky (stars_bsc5.csv) can show that. A sight of the star 'fixes which way is north, not where the ship is' (playability_and_fun.md 3.2). Not in June or July: the northern nights are too light.
cards.when: under_way and level_kind = ocean and (hour >= 22 or hour < 3) and fog < 0.3 and storm < 0.2

cards.title: The ship-star
cards.intention: A clear night with no moon. The stars are so thick that the mast seems to stir them. One of them, low in the north, has hardly moved since dusk.

options.label: Steer by it through the night (likely)
Have the steersman show you the star and the Wagon (sure)
Lie to until daylight (sure)

memory.learn: asked to be shown the ship-star

cards.note: Landfall on the wrong headland: 'the voyage's classic mistake and it is survivable: the chart was wrong, not the world' (playability_and_fun.md 3.2). Ohthere's way: pilotage by the land in sight and which hand it lay on, progress counted in days (Old English Orosius, c. 890). The card never comes within a day of a good mark (flag sea_marks_taken, from the sun, the star, the birds or the fog cards).

cards.title: The wrong headland
cards.intention: Dawn shows land where land should be. But the headland is the wrong shape: too low, with a notch in it that nobody knows, and a river mouth where the steersman's memory has a beach.

options.label: Coast along until a mark you know comes up (sure)
Land a man to ask where you are (likely)
Trust your first reckoning and stand on (doubtful)

cards.note: Land found by the nose, in the hay months (haymaking: wildlife_and_seasons.md 2.10, days 160-200). A seaman's sign of every age; nothing of our period records it (?).

cards.title: The smell of land
cards.intention: The wind has come round off a land you cannot see, and it has brought the land with it: cut hay, peat smoke, cattle. The men lift their heads like dogs.

options.label: Turn up into the smell and close the land (likely)
Hold your course: you know now which side the land lies (sure)

cards.note: A fish weir. Stake-and-wattle weirs of the 7th to 9th centuries stand in the Blackwater and Thames estuaries (?); Dorestad's charters grant fisheries, and its fish bone is full of eel (wildlife_and_seasons.md 1.2: piscationes, 19 species). Six pennies is the fisherman's own price for his stakes, not a law we know (?).

cards.title: A weir in the channel
cards.intention: Stakes across the shallows ahead, with wattle woven between them in a long V and a basket at the point: somebody's fish weir, built farther out into the channel than it has any right to be.

options.label: Go round by the narrow water, slowly (sure)
Buy eels from his basket, for two pennies (sure)
Push through the end of the wattle: she will ride over it (doubtful)

memory.through.success: rode over the end of his weir
memory.through.failure: broke his weir and paid for it

cards.note: Towing upstream. The Utrecht ship has a small mast step near the bow that suggests towing; a towed boat makes about 18 km a day against the stream (ship_physics.md 1.5, 2.9). Men on the rope are the sure form; oxen on a tow path in 793 are our guess (?). NEEDS a variable for the stream (with her or against her): tonight the card can only ask for a place level and no wind, so it can come on still water.

options.label: Pay him two pennies to tow you (sure)
Put two of your own men on the bank with the rope (sure)
Anchor and wait for a wind (sure)
